summary: For ages 4-6 (Reception/Y1), build flexible decomposition of numbers up to 10 into part-pairs (part-part-whole): 5 = 0+5 = 1+4 = 2+3, and their reversals. The core insight is that one whole is a FAMILY of pairs — the whole stays constant while the two parts trade. Fix the whole, systematically vary the split, and record each as an equation, connecting to number bonds and missing-part subtraction. Several complementary formats each play a role: concrete manipulatives and a screen part-whole bench both let the child generate pairs and feel the whole conserved, while a static anchor diagram and recognition checks consolidate the bond facts. Physical manipulation is emphasised at this age in line with the curriculum.
misconceptions: Thinking a number has only ONE decomposition (e.g. 5 is 'just' 4 and 1) and not seeing it as a family of pairs.
Losing the whole — changing a part but not compensating the other, so the total drifts (5 becomes 2+4).
Missing pairs or double-counting when not working systematically, so 'all the ways' is never securely established.
Treating 2+3 and 3+2 as entirely unrelated rather than the same pair reordered.
Not connecting decomposition to subtraction — failing to see that if 5 = 2 + 3 then 5 − 2 = 3.

activities.title: Part-whole bench: slide the divider, keep the whole
steps: Place a fixed whole of counters (e.g. 5) into a single frame, then move a divider across so the counters fall into two parts.
Slide the divider to a new spot and read the two parts aloud (e.g. 1 and 4; then 2 and 3).
Record each split as an equation (5 = 1 + 4, 5 = 2 + 3, …) next to a drawing of the two groups.
Keep a running list of pairs found and check whether every pair has been discovered.
In a 'make 10' mode, fix the whole at 10 and find pairs that make ten.
Flip a found pair to subtraction: having built 5 = 2 + 3, state that 5 − 2 = 3.
activities.insight: A number is not one fixed pair but a whole family of pairs; the parts trade while the total is conserved, and each known pair also tells a missing-part subtraction fact.

activities.title: Physical trading with counters and a part-whole frame
steps: Lay out a fixed whole of two-colour counters or a bead string and physically move one counter from one part to the other.
After each move, say the two parts and write the matching equation.
Build a systematic list of all pairs for 5, then for 10, recording each with a drawing and an equation.
Explain in your own words why the total stays the same when a counter moves across.
Show that 2+3 and 3+2 use the same two groups reordered.
activities.insight: Physically trading objects between two parts of a fixed whole makes conservation tangible: the total never changes, only how it is split.

activities.title: Anchor diagram and recognition checks
steps: Study a part-whole (cherry/bar) diagram for one number and reveal each pair in turn (tap or lift-the-flap 'another way?').
Fill in the missing part: 5 = 2 + __, and set a slider or write the number to complete the bond.

From a set of candidate pairs that also contains a distractor pair whose total is off by one (so it does not make 5), multi-select only the pairs that make 5; the distractor should be left unselected.
Match given pairs to the correct whole.
activities.insight: Seeing several decompositions laid out and practising missing-part completion consolidates number-bond facts and helps spot pairs that do not make the target whole.

checkQuestion: Show me a way to split these 5 counters into two groups. Now show me a DIFFERENT way. How many different ways do you think you can make 5?
checkAnswer: Several ways — 1+4, 2+3, 0+5 (and their reversals). A child who understands part-part-whole generates more than one split and recognises that the whole (5) stays the same while the parts change.
